screens.title: Testing Advanced dApp Features
screens.subtitle: Layered testing for contracts and frontend to ensure secure, reliable dApps

narration.text: Testing a dApp requires more than quick manual checks. In decentralized applications, smart contract bugs are often permanent and costly, so you need a layered approach: unit tests for contract logic and events, integration tests that validate interaction between contracts, and end-to-end tests that exercise the full user flow from UI to chain. You will also learn how to mock Web3 providers so frontend unit tests run fast and deterministic. Practically, we’ll examine how Hardhat and Truffle help assert event emissions, how to run E2E flows against a local Ganache or Hardhat node, and how to stub Web3. js in Jest so UI components behave predictably. A common misunderstanding is thinking unit tests alone are enough; they catch logic errors but not integration or UX issues. By the end of this chapter you’ll know how to combine assertions for events, scripted E2E flows for wallet interactions, and lightweight provider mocks to achieve fast feedback. Consider which test type you’d run first when you push a new contract change and why that order matters.

keyIdea.title: Layer your tests
keyIdea.text: Use unit tests for contract logic and events, E2E for user flows with a local chain, and mocks for fast frontend unit testing.

This chapter takes you from asserting event payloads in unit tests to running Cypress-style E2E tests against Ganache or Hardhat Network, then shows how to mock Web3 for fast frontend tests. Each topic includes examples and common pitfalls.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand how to design and run tests that protect both on-chain and off-chain parts of a dApp. You will be able to write unit tests for smart contracts that validate emitted events and state changes, so off-chain listeners receive accurate data. You will also implement end-to-end tests that automate wallet interactions and verify UI updates against a local blockchain, preventing integration regressions. Finally, you will learn to mock Web3. js providers and contract instances so frontend unit tests are deterministic and fast, avoiding slow network calls during component testing. Each objective is practical: from using assertion helpers in Hardhat to scripting Cypress flows that confirm a user can mint tokens and see their balance update. A common misconception is treating mocking as a shortcut rather than a deliberate tool: mocks verify UI behavior quickly but must be complemented by integration or E2E tests that exercise real chain interactions. These objectives prepare you to assemble a testing pipeline that balances speed, coverage, and realism.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.subtitle: How you will apply the testing concepts in real projects

narration.text: These practical goals focus on technique and workflow. First, you’ll script smart contract unit tests that include event checks so your UI and backend can rely on precise event payloads. Second, you’ll prepare a reproducible local blockchain environment—either Ganache or Hardhat Network—and use it to deploy contracts and run E2E scenarios. Third, you’ll implement frontend unit tests that replace real Web3 providers with mocks, returning predictable values for calls, sends, and events. Finally, you’ll structure a testing suite for continuous integration so tests run automatically on changes. For example, you might run fast frontend and contract unit tests on every commit, and trigger a full integration + E2E pipeline for pull requests. A frequent misconception is thinking mocks eliminate the need for E2E tests; in reality, mocks speed up developer feedback but must be validated with real or local-chain integration tests. These objectives will help you balance speed, coverage, and confidence when releasing dApp updates.

screens.title: Why rigorous testing matters for dApps
screens.subtitle: Security, immutability, and financial risk demand layered testing

narration.text: Blockchain transactions are immutable. That means a bug discovered after deployment often cannot be fixed without a costly migration. Rigorous testing reduces that risk. Start by defining what each test layer protects: unit tests check the smallest pieces of logic in isolation, integration tests verify interactions between contracts or between backend components, and end-to-end tests validate the real user journey from UI to chain. A concrete example: an ERC-20 transfer function could pass unit checks for balance calculations but still emit the wrong event arguments; without event assertions, off-chain listeners may process incorrect data and mis-update user interfaces. A common misconception is that test coverage as a percentage guarantees correctness. Coverage is a signal, not a proof. Instead, focus tests on critical financial paths and access control checks. To build tests effectively, choose tools that let you assert events and state, run a local chain for fast iteration, and mock slow external systems where appropriate. Reflect: which part of your dApp would be most harmful if it failed on mainnet, and how would you protect it with these layered tests?

keyIdea.title: Protect the irreversible
keyIdea.text: Prioritize tests for paths that change funds or permissions; event assertions ensure off-chain systems stay consistent.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Why rigorous testing matters for dApps
Definition

Rigorous testing means matching test depth to risk: unit tests for correctness, integration to ensure components talk correctly, and E2E for real user journeys that touch signing, gas, and UI state.

Analogy
Think of tests like safety checks on a bridge: individual bolts, the connecting plates, and full-load trials each play a role.
Concrete example
A token transfer that passes arithmetic checks but emits wrong event args can cause UI to show incorrect balances.
Common mistake
Relying only on unit tests for speed and skipping E2E validation against a local chain.
Key Takeaway

Layer tests by risk: protect token movements, access control, and event payloads that drive off-chain behavior.

Try this

Identify one critical function in your dApp and write a unit test that asserts both its state change and the emitted event arguments.

screens.title: Unit testing smart contract events with Hardhat
screens.subtitle: Assert emitted events and their arguments to keep off-chain listeners reliable

narration.text: Event assertions are essential because events are the contract's primary contract-to-off-chain signal. When a dApp listens to events for UI updates or backend processing, wrong or missing event data breaks downstream logic. In Hardhat you can use assertion helpers to check both that an event was emitted and that it carried specific arguments. For example, when testing a token transfer, your test should mint tokens where needed, call transfer, and assert that a Transfer event is emitted with the correct sender, recipient, and amount. A common misconception is that checking balances alone is sufficient; balances confirm state, but they do not guarantee event payload integrity. The code example is a minimal Hardhat test that deploys MyToken, mints tokens to the owner, calls transfer, and uses expect(). to. emit(). withArgs() to assert the event. Run such tests frequently during contract development. After listening to this, ask yourself: which events in your contract are relied on by the frontend, and are they covered by unit tests? Unit testing smart contract events with Hardhat means use expect().to.emit() to verify events and payloads so off-chain code receives correct signals.. In practical terms, assert emitted events and their arguments to keep off-chain listeners reliable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assert events
keyIdea.text: Use expect().to.emit() to verify events and payloads so off-chain code receives correct signals.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Unit testing smart contract events with Hardhat
What to assert
  • That the event was emitted on the expected transaction.
  • That the event's return values match the expected addresses and amounts.
  • That related state changes (balances, allowances) are correct.
Misconception check

Do not assume state verification alone guarantees correct event payloads. Events drive off-chain behavior and must be tested directly.

Hardhat test example
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("MyToken", function () {
  let MyToken, myToken, owner, addr1;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
    MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
    myToken = await MyToken.deploy();
    await myToken.waitForDeployment();
  });

  it("Should emit Transfer event on token transfer", async function () {
    await myToken.mint(owner.address, 100);
    await expect(myToken.transfer(addr1.address, 50))
      .to.emit(myToken, "Transfer")
      .withArgs(owner.address, addr1.address, 50);
  });
});
Note: Run with a Hardhat test runner that includes chai-ethers matchers.
Takeaway

Test both state and events. Events are the contract's API to the off-chain world and must be correct.

screens.title: Setting up E2E tests with a local blockchain
screens.subtitle: Repeatable environments using Ganache or Hardhat Network

narration.text: End-to-end tests need a predictable blockchain environment. For that we run a local node like Ganache or Hardhat Network. The typical workflow is: first, start a local node in a separate terminal and deploy your contracts there. Second, seed accounts with test funds to simulate real users. Third, launch your app pointed at the local RPC so the UI talks to the test chain. Fourth, use a browser automation tool to script interactions and confirm wallet operations. This gives you fast, isolated tests that do not depend on public testnets. A concrete example: run npx hardhat node, deploy MyToken, and then use Cypress to visit the app and perform the deposit or mint flows. A common mistake is relying on a shared test network that others modify; using a local node isolates your suite and makes results reproducible. Finally, decide which flows need full wallet confirmation and which can use a testing account that signs transactions programmatically for simpler automation. Setting up E2E tests with a local blockchain means use a local, ephemeral blockchain for repeatable e2e tests to avoid external network variability.. In practical terms, repeatable environments using ganache or hardhat network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Local chain, predictable tests

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Setting up E2E tests with a local blockchain
E2E Setup Steps
1. Start a local node: run Ganache or npx hardhat node to provide predictable RPC and funded accounts for testing.
2. Deploy contracts: run your deployment script against the local chain so contract addresses are stable during the test run.
3. Seed accounts: fund test wallets with ETH and any tokens needed for flows like deposit or mint.
4. Point your app: configure the dApp to use http://localhost:8545 so UI communicates with the test node.
5. Automate browser actions: use Cypress or Playwright plus wallet automation to confirm transactions and assert final UI state.
Misconception: local nodes are only for development. In fact, they are essential for reliable E2E testing because they give you deterministic, isolated test runs that can be reproduced in CI.
Concrete example

Start Hardhat node, deploy MyToken, visit the app at localhost, then script a mint transaction and verify the displayed balance updates to the minted amount.

Check your understanding

screens.title: Automating wallet interactions during E2E tests
screens.subtitle: Tools and strategies to confirm transactions and connect wallets

narration.text: E2E tests often need to interact with a wallet to sign transactions. There are two main strategies: automate the actual browser wallet extension or use a direct signer for testing. Automating a browser extension, for example with a Cypress plugin that controls MetaMask, gives the closest simulation of a real user flow. Tools can accept access, confirm transactions, and return control to the test. Alternatively, for simpler flows, configure the dApp under test to use a programmatic account created from a private key. That approach avoids UI wallet prompts but must only be used in tests because it exposes keys. A concrete scenario: your test clicks Connect, a plugin accepts MetaMask access, the test triggers a mint, then the plugin confirms the transaction so the test can assert balance changes. A common error is leaving test-only private key code in production; always gate programmatic signing behind test configuration. Consider which flows in your app must run with the real extension and which can safely use a test signer for automation speed. Automating wallet interactions during E2E tests means use wallet-extension automation for realism or a programmatic signer for speed, but never ship test keys to production.. In practical terms, tools and strategies to confirm transactions and connect wallets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › E2E test example with Cypress and a local chain
Pseudo-code flow
describe('DApp E2E Flow', () => {
  before(() => {
    // Deploy contracts to local chain and visit dApp
    cy.visit('http://localhost:3000');
  });

  it('connects wallet and displays account', () => {
    cy.get('[data-testid="connect-wallet-button"]').click();
    cy.confirmMetamaskAccess();
    cy.get('[data-testid="connected-account"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('mints tokens and updates balance', () => {
    cy.get('[data-testid="deposit-input"]').type('0.1');
    cy.get('[data-testid="deposit-button"]').click();
    cy.confirmMetamaskTransaction();
    cy.get('[data-testid="balance-display"]').should('contain', '0.1');
  });
});
Notice the test asserts both UI visibility and the balance update, which may be driven by a contract event or direct state read.
Pitfall

Avoid only asserting success messages. Confirming on-chain state or emitted events gives stronger guarantees.

Try this

Extend the test to read a contract method after the transaction and assert the returned value matches the UI.

screens.title: Mocking Web3.js for fast frontend tests
screens.subtitle: Create deterministic contract and provider mocks to avoid slow network calls

narration.text: Frontend unit tests must be fast and deterministic. Hitting a real node slows tests and leads to nondeterministic failures. The solution is to mock the Web3 provider and contract instances so methods like call and send return predefined values or resolved promises. A practical example is creating a mock Web3 object with eth. getAccounts, getChainId, and a mocked Contract class with methods. myViewFunction. call returning a resolved value. You can also mock events to simulate on-event callbacks by invoking the provided callback in a setTimeout inside the mock. A common misunderstanding is that mocks reduce the need for integration tests; they do not. Mocks speed up component development and catch UI-level regressions quickly, but you must still validate integration with a real or local chain. When implementing mocks, make them minimal and predictable: return values that represent realistic chain responses and test both success and failure modes so components behave correctly under error conditions. Mocking Web3.js for fast frontend tests means mock web3 calls and events to keep frontend unit tests fast, predictable, and suitable for ci.. In practical terms, create deterministic contract and provider mocks to avoid slow network calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mock for speed
keyIdea.text: Mock Web3 calls and events to keep frontend unit tests fast, predictable, and suitable for CI.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Mocking Web3.js for fast frontend tests
Mock structure
  • Mock provider methods: getAccounts, getChainId, and helpers like toWei/fromWei if used.
  • Mock Contract: implement a methods object whose functions return objects with call or send that resolve test values.
  • Mock events: provide an events object that allows on('data', cb) to trigger callbacks with simulated payloads.
Test both normal and failure responses so UI handles errors gracefully, for example when call() rejects or send() fails.
Mock example
const mockWeb3 = {
  eth: {
    getAccounts: jest.fn(() => Promise.resolve(['0xMockAccount'])),
    getChainId: jest.fn(() => Promise.resolve(1337)),
    Contract: jest.fn(() => ({
      methods: {
        myViewFunction: jest.fn(() => ({ call: jest.fn(() => Promise.resolve('Mocked View Data')) })),
        myMutateFunction: jest.fn(() => ({ send: jest.fn(() => Promise.resolve({ transactionHash: '0xMockTxHash' })) })),
      },
      events: {
        MyEvent: jest.fn(() => ({ on: jest.fn((event, callback) => { if (event === 'data') { setTimeout(() => callback({ event: 'MyEvent', returnValues: { arg1: 'mockValue' }, transactionHash: '0xmockEventTx' }), 100); } return { unsubscribe: jest.fn() }; }) })),
    })),
  },
  utils: { fromWei: jest.fn((val) => val), toWei: jest.fn((val) => val) },
};

jest.mock('web3', () => jest.fn(() => mockWeb3));
Takeaway

Mocks speed tests and let you simulate on-event behavior; pair them with integration tests to be confident about real chain interactions.

screens.title: Mocks vs. Local Chain vs. Mainnet testing
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs: speed, realism, and isolation

narration.text: When designing your test suite, you must balance three axes: speed, realism, and isolation. Mocks are the fastest option and offer isolation from network variability, making them ideal for frequent unit tests. Local chains like Ganache or Hardhat Network give strong realism for contract behavior and integration but are slower than mocks. Mainnet or public testnets give the most realistic environment but are non-deterministic and slow; they are best for final staging, not every commit. Consider an example workflow: run mocks for frontend component tests on every commit, run contract unit tests and short integration checks on pull requests, and schedule full E2E runs on a protected branch or nightly CI that uses a local chain. A common misconception is thinking you must choose one approach; in practice you combine them. The right mix provides quick developer feedback through mocks and asserts real behavior through local-chain E2E tests before deployment. Mocks vs. Local Chain vs. Mainnet testing means use mocks for speed, local chains for integration realism, and reserve public networks for final staging.. In practical terms, trade-offs: speed, realism, and isolation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mix approaches
keyIdea.text: Use mocks for speed, local chains for integration realism, and reserve public networks for final staging.

screens.title: Designing a robust testing suite
screens.subtitle: Structure tests for speed, clarity, and CI integration

narration.text: A well-structured test suite separates concerns and optimizes for developer productivity. Organize tests into folders: contract unit tests, backend/integration tests, frontend unit tests with mocks, and E2E tests that run against a local chain. In CI, run fast frontend and contract unit tests on each push, and gate slower E2E and integration suites behind pull requests or nightly runs. Use realistic but non-production data in tests and include edge cases such as insufficient funds, incorrect permissions, and contract reverts. Another useful practice is to seed the local chain with deterministic accounts and balances so E2E tests can run without manual setup. Keep tests small and focused—each test should verify one behavior. Finally, use code coverage to guide testing gaps but don’t chase 100% blindly; focus on critical paths and business logic. A misconception is that more tests always equal more confidence; poorly designed slow tests reduce developer velocity and are often ignored. Balance quality and speed so tests remain a helpful safety net. Designing a robust testing suite means keep tests small, focused, and organized by layer; run fast checks often and heavy e2e tests on controlled schedules.. In practical terms, structure tests for speed, clarity, and ci integration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Structure matters
keyIdea.text: Keep tests small, focused, and organized by layer; run fast checks often and heavy E2E tests on controlled schedules.

Recommended structure
/tests/contracts
Unit tests for contract functions and event assertions.
/tests/frontend
Component tests with mocked Web3 and simulated events.
/tests/integration
Backend and contract interaction tests that validate integration points.
/tests/e2e

In CI, run fast unit tests on every commit and schedule or gate full E2E runs to avoid long-running pipelines on every push.

  • Access control violations and reverts.

After the transaction completes, assert the UI balance shows the minted amount and optionally verify the balance directly by calling the contract from the test runner. A common mistake is neglecting to deploy the contract before running the test; make deployment part of your before or CI setup. This activity helps you practice deploying to a local chain, automating wallet confirmations, and writing assertions that check both UI and contract state. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › E2E activity: Test a token mint flow
Activity checklist
  1. Initialize Hardhat and add MyToken.sol to contracts.
  2. Run npx hardhat node and deploy with the provided deploy.js script.
  3. Start your React dApp pointed at http://localhost:8545 and confirm contract address is configured.
  4. Write a Cypress test that connects MetaMask, clicks Mint, confirms the transaction, and asserts the UI balance updates to 100 MTK.
  5. Optionally verify contract balance via web3 call in the test to confirm on-chain state.
Remember to seed accounts and include a before hook in tests that deploys contracts so runs are repeatable in CI.
Starter deploy script
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
  const myToken = await MyToken.deploy();
  await myToken.waitForDeployment();
  console.log("MyToken deployed to:", await myToken.getAddress());
}

main();
Common pitfall

Forgetting to update the dApp's token address after redeploying locally will make tests fail; always wire deployment address into your test setup.

screens.title: Best practices for reliable and fast tests
screens.subtitle: Automate, separate, realistic data, and focus on critical paths

narration.text: A few practical rules make test suites sustainable. First, automate everything: run tests in CI to avoid drift and manual steps. Second, keep a clear separation between contract, backend, and frontend tests so each layer can be executed independently. Third, use realistic but non-production data and seed accounts deterministically in local chains so tests remain reproducible. Fourth, prioritize tests by risk: money-moving actions and access control deserve more and deeper tests than cosmetic UI interactions. Fifth, mock slow external services to keep unit tests fast but still include integration runs that use real or local chains. Finally, monitor test performance—slow tests that provide little value should be refactored or moved to scheduled runs. A common mistake is bloating the suite with redundant tests; prefer smaller, focused tests that validate a single behavior. Ask yourself: which tests would you remove or change to speed feedback while preserving safety for critical flows? Best practices for reliable and fast tests means automate in ci, separate tests by layer, seed realistic data, and focus effort where financial or security risk is highest.. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Best practices for reliable and fast tests
Core practices
  • Automate tests in CI and make runs reproducible with seeded local chains.
  • Separate tests by layer so failures are easy to diagnose and fix.
  • Mock slow external calls, but validate integration with local-chain E2E runs.
  • Focus coverage on financial paths, access control, and events that drive the UI.
Keep tests focused and fast. Use coverage metrics to find gaps, but let critical business logic guide where to spend effort.
Checklist
  1. Are critical flows covered by both unit and E2E tests?
  2. Do frontend unit tests use mocks for speed?
  3. Are integration tests reproducible in CI with local chain deployment?
Pro tip

Run quick mock-based tests on every commit and reserve slower local-chain E2E runs for PR verification or nightly builds.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from Testing Advanced dApp Features

narration.text: Remember these three core ideas. First, unit tests must include event assertions because events are how off-chain systems react; verify both state and emitted payloads. Second, end-to-end tests running against a local blockchain validate the full user journey including wallet confirmations and UI updates—this catches integration issues that unit tests miss. Third, mocking Web3 providers keeps frontend unit tests fast and deterministic, but mocks are complements, not replacements, for integration and E2E tests. Together they form a practical, layered testing strategy: fast mocks for development feedback, local-chain integration for correctness, and targeted mainnet staging for final validation. Second, use a local blockchain for E2E tests so you can script wallet confirmations and assert on-chain results without network noise. Use this triad to build a testing strategy that is both fast for developers and thorough enough to catch dangerous regressions.
